what: Brookfield Renewable Corporation owns power plants that generate electricity without fuel: hydroelectric dams, wind farms, solar installations and battery storage, across North and South America, Europe and Asia. It sells the electricity under long contracts, mostly to utilities and large corporate buyers.
customers: Electric utilities buying power under long-term agreements, and increasingly large corporations — particularly technology companies — contracting directly for clean electricity to supply their data centres.
money: Long-established dams with very long asset lives and low operating costs.
Onshore and offshore wind and solar generation under power purchase agreements.
Battery storage, pumped hydro and distributed generation.
moat: Hydroelectric dams are the best generating assets in existence: they last a century, cost almost nothing to run, and new ones essentially cannot be built because the sites and permits are gone. Beyond that, the revenue comes from contracts lasting a decade or more with inflation adjustment, which makes the cash flow unusually predictable for an electricity producer.
risks: A trailing net loss of $1.3B and free cash flow of about negative $795.0M — the accounting for depreciation and project-level financing makes the reported figures very difficult to read.
Debt of $15.6B against $682.0M of cash is enormous, and renewable projects are financed with borrowing against their contracted revenue.
Rising interest rates hurt twice: they raise financing costs on new projects and reduce what the contracted cash flows are worth.
Revenue declined from $4.1B in 2024 to $3.7B in 2025.
Hydroelectric output depends on rainfall, which varies and has become less predictable.
opportunities: EV/EBITDA of 10.5 is a reasonable multiple for contracted power generation assets.
Long-term power purchase agreements with inflation adjustment produce genuinely predictable cash flow.
Data centre electricity demand is creating a new class of corporate buyer willing to sign long contracts at good prices.
Hydroelectric capacity is irreplaceable: the sites are taken and new dams are not permitted.
Seven analysts average a $37.71 target, about 24% above the current price.
watch: Funds from operations per share and the contracted share of generation. Reported earnings are unusable for this asset class; the contracted cash flow and what it costs per share are what matter.
view: The first thing to establish about Brookfield Renewable is that its reported earnings cannot be used. A trailing net loss of $1.3 billion and negative free cash flow look like a failing business and describe something quite different: heavy depreciation on long-lived assets whose economic life far exceeds their accounting life, plus project-level financing and capital spending on construction. The right measures are funds from operations per share and the contracted share of generation. Anyone looking at the net income line here will reach a conclusion that bears no relationship to the assets.

Those assets are genuinely good, and the hydroelectric portfolio is the best part by a wide margin. A dam lasts a century, costs almost nothing to operate, and cannot be replicated — the sites are taken and new large dams are not permitted in most of the developed world. That is an irreplaceable position, and it is why hydro deserves a materially higher multiple than wind or solar, which are manufactured assets anyone with capital can build.

The business model’s weakness is its dependence on borrowing. Renewable projects are financed against their contracted revenue, which means $15.6 billion of debt and a structure where interest rates hurt twice over: they raise the cost of building new projects and reduce the present value of the contracted cash flows already owned. That is why the whole sector derated when rates rose, and it was a rational response rather than a mood.

The newer development that genuinely changes the picture is data centre demand. Technology companies need large amounts of electricity, want it to be clean, and are willing to sign long contracts at prices that would have been unthinkable five years ago. That gives owners of existing generation — particularly dispatchable hydro — a counterparty class that did not previously exist. At 10.5 times EV/EBITDA with seven analysts seeing 24% of upside, this is a reasonable price for contracted cash flow from irreplaceable assets, provided the holder understands they are buying a leveraged infrastructure vehicle rather than a utility stock, and judges it on funds from operations per share.
bull: Data centre buyers sign long contracts at strong prices for irreplaceable hydro and existing renewables, while falling rates lift the value of contracted cash flow.
bear: Rates stay high against $15.6 billion of debt, new project economics do not clear, and dry years cut hydro output on a vehicle with no earnings cushion.
